title: #64 If You Wrote This, Put Your Boards Down
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Barton returns to the challenge of processing 30 mini-whiteboards' worth of data within the few seconds a check for understanding typically allows. He recaps two standard mitigations -- controlling the flow of information by checking boards row by row, and reducing the data itself by asking only for a final answer or a single step -- before describing a technique he saw on a school visit that combines both. Working through a grid-method multiplication problem, the teacher asked students to reveal their answer to just one square of the grid, then, on seeing an answer on his own board, invited any students who had written that same answer to put their boards down. Because the pool of remaining boards shrank each time he identified a matching answer, he could rapidly cycle through all the distinct responses in the room without needing to compare all 30 boards against each other simultaneously.
points: Standard fixes for whiteboard overload -- checking row by row, or asking for only the final answer -- reduce data volume but still require scanning the whole class at once.

The observed technique adds a dynamic filtering step: naming an answer the teacher can see and asking matching students to put their boards down actively shrinks the pool of boards still needing review.

Because each round of "put your boards down if you wrote this" isolates one distinct answer at a time, the teacher can identify and address all four answers in the room without needing to process 30 boards simultaneously.
The technique works because it turns a passive visual scan into an interactive elimination process, making the whole-class check faster without sacrificing accuracy.
quotes: It can be challenging to take in the data of 30 boards in front of you in the few seconds usually allocated for such a check for understanding.
Control the flow of information - ask for the students on the back row to show you their boards first, then the next row, and so on
Reduce the amount of data to be processed - only ask students to show you the final answer or a single step in a solution
In such circumstances, it would be easy to miss an answer or two despite reducing the amount of data to be processed. But the teacher did something smart.
Every time he wrote an answer he could see on his board, he asked any students who had also written that answer to put their boards down.
This further reduced the amount of data to be processed, and meant that he could spot and subsequently address each of the four answers in the room.
